title: Instruction Resilience Bench — personal lab notes
content:
Topline: exploratory scratchpad for assembling a small, portable bench to stress-test instruction-following behavior across prompt variants and few-shot packs. Goal is not to replace Eval infra, but to iterate fast on prompt families and capture brittle modes before they reach customer-facing templates.

Motivation / quick context:
- Observed small regressions when switching to quantized variants (esp 4-bit) where short imperative instructions are ignored intermittently. Need a reproducible small harness to pinpoint failure classes.
- Want to codify a few-shot ’immune system’ for prompts: a set of exemplar shots and fallback transforms that reduce catastrophic instruction-dropping.

Basic plan (iterative):
1) Curate 6–8 micro-tasks that are representative of product surface areas (summarization, classification, normalize-persona, redact PHI, format to JSON, extract entities). Keep prompts <= 3 instructions each.
2) For each micro-task, design 5 prompt families: baseline (short), anchored (explicit role + step numbers), redundant (repeat critical directive), contrastive shotset (good/bad examples), minimal exemplar (1-shot).
3) Run across model variants we care about (open-1, redwood-v1-small, quantized variants), capture: instruction-follow-rate, hallucination rate, output-format-fidelity, avg tokens, and a qualitative failure tag (e.g., omission, diversion, hallucination, format-breach).
4) Automated triage: tag failures and map to suggested transforms (prepend anchor, increase exemplar weight, add negative example).

Micro-task list (seed):
- Task A: "Summarize in one sentence" (explicit compressive summary)
- Task B: "Extract customer-support fields" (name, date, issue, priority) -> structured JSON
- Task C: "Redact PII" (remove emails, phone numbers, show redaction markers)
- Task D: "Tone shift" (convert neutral -> enthusiastic with three bullets)
- Task E: "Few-line policy justification" (2-3 sentences, cite policy tag optional)
- Task F: "Single-step code edit" (given a short JS snippet, apply a one-line change)

Prompt family sketches (examples):
- Baseline-short (B1): "Summarize the following in one sentence:\n[TEXT]"
- Anchored-step (A1): "You are an assistant that MUST follow instructions exactly.\nStep 1: Read text.\nStep 2: Provide a one-sentence summary.\nOutput must be a single sentence, no extra commentary.\n[TEXT]"
- Redundant-directive (R1): "Summarize in one sentence. Do not add examples, do not explain. Only one sentence.\n[TEXT]"
- Contrastive-shot (C1): "Good: \nInput: 'Short review' -> Summary: 'Positive: concise'\nBad: \nInput: 'Long review' -> Response: 'I think...' (avoid)\nNow produce a one-sentence summary for: [TEXT]"
- Minimal-1shot (M1): "Example:\nInput: 'X' -> 'Y'\nNow: [TEXT]"

Quick few-shot set (Task B structured extraction) example:
- 3 positive exemplars: mapping free text -> {name, date, issue, priority}
- 2 negative exemplars: show wrong field mapping (to expose model to failure)
Rationale: expose both correct shape and common mis-parses.

Failure cases I've already seen (notes):
- Omission: model returns a summary but drops named entities required for JSON extraction. Happens at longer inputs (> 250 tokens).
- Format-drift: model returns pretty prose instead of strict JSON (common on quantized variants).
- Directive-ignore: model answers with general advice instead of applying instruction (happens with shorter baseline prompts).
- Hallucinated fields: invents dates or contact details not in text (rare but present).

Measurements to capture in bench (minimal schema):
- instr_follow_rate: percent outputs that satisfy instruction constraints (format + content)
- format_success: whether expected JSON or single-sentence rule respected
- hallucination_flag: yes/no (manual label or heuristics)
- avg_tokens: mean tokens generated
- latency_ms: median latency (for quick perf check)
- failure_tag: list of tags per failure
- prompt_variant: which family run

Small test harness notes:
- Keep seed corpus small (80 examples total: ~12–15 per micro-task) for fast iteration. Use stratified lengths (short/med/long).
- Randomize noise: insert parenthetical asides, emojis, inline code samples to stress parsing.
- Re-run nightly for targeted models; export CSV summary and a small sample set of failing cases.

Edge experiments to try (cheap):
- Prepend a single sentence: "You are held to 1-sentence output or you will return FAIL." (stress test for token-truncation/stop behavior)
- Add a trailing explicit token: "###END###" to encourage deterministic stop; measure effect on format_success
- Use negative examples in contrastive pairs: showing what NOT to do seems to reduce hallucination in some runs. Empirical only.

Concrete prompt snippets to record (for quick copy):
- "Assistant MUST follow the structure exactly. If you cannot, output EXACTLY: FAILED-STRUCTURE."
- "Return only JSON. Do not include backticks, markdown or commentary."
- "If information is missing, set the field value to null or the string 'MISSING'."

Quick checklist for next session:
- [ ] codify 80-example seed set and commit to repo (see linked PR above)
- [ ] implement harness that captures instr_follow_rate + failure_tag in CSV
- [ ] run bench across 3 model variants and 2 quantization modes
- [ ] review top 20 failing prompts and manually craft 2 remedial prompt transforms each
- [ ] check for drift after applying remedial transforms (A/B within-harness)

Notes to self / TODO bullets (freeform):
- Try adding a "role play" frame where assistant is a compliance auditor vs a creative writer and see whether role anchoring reduces hallucination.
- Ask Maya to add a small set of customer transcripts (anonymized) for extraction tests.
- Jonah: can you wire up a quick notebook that pulls model variants from the staging catalog and returns CSV? Slack @jonah for infra tokens.
- Keep this bench intentionally small and human-review heavy — product wants low false-negatives (don’t ship obviously broken prompts).

Open questions / hypotheses worth testing:
- H1: explicit negative examples reduce hallucination more than extra positive exemplars. (Design: compare +1 negative vs +1 positive)
- H2: anchored step numbering reduces omission but increases verbosity; measure token cost tradeoff.
- H3: quantized small models benefit more from redundant directives than anchored steps.

References / quick links:
- Linear task RED-2312 (prompt regression triage)
- GH eval harness PR #89 (seed corpus + parser)
- Slack thread: #prompt-regression (see 2026-01-14 thread re: format drift)

Scratchpad end — keep iterating. If this shows signal, extract top 3 transforms and fold into the prompt template library (lightweight, TTR-sensible).

-- E.N. (notes are deliberately terse; push back if need a full doc for product)
